<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Nikema Williams>: The bill would amend the Economic Growth and Regulatory Paperwork Reduction Act of 1996 (``EGRPRA'') to increase the frequency of a comprehensive regulatory review conducted every 10 years by Federal banking regulators to every 5 years and require them to conduct a further review of the cumulative impact of their regulations with additional cost-benefit analysis that ignores certain benefits, like consumer protection. As described in more detail below, the EGRPRA process is already an elaborate one, with extensive stakeholder engagement that typically last three years. Moreover, regulators already have authority to update rules whenever it may be appropriate, and doing an exhaustive regulatory review every 5 years would distract regulators from their day-to-day duties to oversee the banking system.
EGRPRA requires the federal banking regulators--Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (``Fed''), Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (``FDIC''), and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (``OCC'') that serve on the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council (``FFIEC'' or ``Council'') to conduct a review not less frequently than every ten years, ``of all regulations prescribed by the Council or by any such appropriate Federal banking agency, respectively, in order to identify outdated or otherwise unnecessary regulatory requirements imposed on insured depository institutions.''\1\ While the National Credit Union Administration (``NCUA'') is not technically covered by EGRPRA, the NCUA has voluntarily participated in the EGRPRA regulatory review process in the past. This bill would codify that practice to include NCUA in the requirement.
\1\FFIEC, Economic Growth and Regulatory Paperwork Reduction Act (accessed Dec. 13, 2025).
To date, there have been two major EGRPRA reviews and reports, with the first one issued in July 2007 and the second released in March 2017.\2\ The agencies have already begun working on a third one. Even though the law does not prevent the regulators from conducting the EGRPRA review more frequently than once every 10 years, that is the cadence the regulators have followed given the fact it takes several years to conduct outreach and do the analysis to produce the report. Using the last round as an example, the federal banking agencies initially sought public comment to identify outdated, unnecessary, or unduly burdensome regulations imposed on insured depository institutions in June 2014, and announced in November 2014 that they were conducting a round of outreach meetings to consider stakeholder input into the review.\3\ The resulting EGRPRA report was sent to Congress and published in March 2017, nearly three years after the review was initiated. Moreover, regulators already have authority to update rules whenever appropriate, and requiring an exhaustive EGRPRA process more frequently, such as every 5 years instead of 10 years, would likely distract regulators from their regular responsibilities to oversee the banking system.
\2\Id.
\3\Id.
Moreover, the bill requires each agency to do a cumulative impact cost-benefit analysis of all of their rules, though it appears that elements of the review are slanted to focus on compliance burdens and not account for regulatory benefits, like consumer protection. This bill would require agencies to publish their findings, and given that courts have acted to increasingly restrain what Federal regulators can do, this analysis could be used by industry in suing to block the implementation of the agency's rulemakings.\4\
\4\See John C. Coates, IV, Cost-Benefit Analysis of Financial Regulation: Case Studies and Implications (Jan. 15, 2015); and Davis Wright Trermaine, New Administration Outlook: Litigation Battles Over Financial Regulations Are Poised To Shift (Nov. 19, 2024).
This bill is somewhat similar to a bill Republicans passed through the House in 2018, though that bill notably shifted the EGRPRA review to 7 years (instead of 5 years, as this new bill proposes) and included the CFPB, which this bill does not.\5\ Moreover, H.R. 6544 is opposed by Americans for Financial Reform.
\5\See H.R. 4607 (115th Cong.), Comprehensive Regulatory Review Act (Loudermilk).
For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 6544.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Al Green,
Bill Foster,
Joyce Beatty,
Rashida Tlaib,
Sylvia R. Garcia,
Nikema Williams,
Members of Congress.
